articles.title: Lloyd’s Register approves new classification rules for nuclear-powered ships
articles.summary: Lloyd’s Register (LR) has approved new classification rules for nuclear-powered ships and offshore units, marking another step towards the potential use of nuclear energy in commercial shipping. The new framework sets out the requirements for assessing how nuclear power systems can be integrated into vessels and...
articles.body: Lloyd’s Register (LR) has approved new classification rules for nuclear-powered ships and offshore units, marking another step towards the potential use of nuclear energy in commercial shipping. The new framework sets out the requirements for assessing how nuclear power systems can be integrated into vessels and offshore facilities. The rules apply to different ship types and nuclear technologies. They do not prescribe a particular reactor design, allowing developers to assess various solutions as the technology advances. According to LR, the framework is believed to be the first developed by a classification society to cover all types of ships and offshore units. The rules have been approved by the organisation’s Ships and Offshore Technical Committees. New framework addresses nuclear integration The classification rules establish goals and technical requirements for integrating nuclear power into maritime applications. They also draw on LR’s existing risk-based certification process, which helps connect maritime classification requirements with nuclear licensing considerations. This approach is intended to support ship designers, operators and technology developers during the early stages of nuclear-powered projects. “Navies have decades of experience with nuclear propulsion, but newer reactor technologies could open up different possibilities for future fleets,” said David Lloyd, Vice President Naval and Government Business, Lloyd’s Register. “These Rules provide a common classification framework for assessing that integration, without prescribing a particular reactor design,” Lloyd added. The framework covers potential applications beyond vessel propulsion, including floating nuclear power units and energy supplies for ports and nearby industries. Mark Tipping, Global Offshore Power-to-X Director at LR, said nuclear power could provide new opportunities for both shipping and offshore operations. “These rules provide a common framework for those developing or bringing forward nuclear maritime projects,” Tipping said. LR is also working with industry organisations and regulators to address the wider requirements for nuclear-powered maritime operations. Its activities include cooperation with the Nuclear Energy Maritime Organization (NEMO) and the British Ports Association. The classification society said the new rules will continue to evolve as nuclear technologies develop and international regulatory requirements become clearer. The framework does not constitute approval for the installation or operation of any specific nuclear reactor or vessel.
takeaways: Lloyd’s Register (LR) has approved new classification rules for nuclear-powered ships and offshore units, marking another step towards the potential use of nuclear energy in commercial shipping.
The new framework sets out the requirements for assessing how nuclear power systems can be integrated into vessels and offshore facilities.

articles.title: ASIA LNG MOC PERFORMANCE: Deliveries conclude for record volume of 148.5 TBtu during August MOC

articles.body: ASIA LNG MOC PERFORMANCE: Deliveries conclude for record volume of 148.5 TBtu during August MOC in General Energy News 21/11/2026 Participants in the Asia LNG Platts Market on Close assessment process concluded physical deliveries for a record volume of 148.5 TBtu during August, according to operational trade performance data compiled by Platts, part of S&P Global Energy. The milestone topples the last high recorded just a month ago, when 34 trades – amounting to 113 TBtu – were concluded for LNG product traded in July. Over the past 10 months of this year, LNG traded volumes have already risen to record highs three times, the first being in January when MOC activity saw 110 TBtu changing hands, Platts data showed. There were 44 trades in total during the August MOC, with volumes rising 29.03% month over month and 61.82% year over year. Shell was the biggest buyer with 82.9 TBtu, while QaterEnergy Trading was the largest seller with 43.3 TBtu, Platts data showed. Participants attributed the rise in MOC activity in part to a persistently closed East-West arbitrage, which limited the flow of marginal US-sourced cargoes into the region. At the same time, demand from South Asian buyers for prompt cargoes also tightened near-term availability, industry sources said. Performance tracking Platts closely monitors the performance of trades reported through the MOC as part of its ongoing commitment to upholding the highest standards of integrity and transparency. As part of performance tracking, Platts reviewed various aspects of performance, including timeliness of nominations, completion of deliveries and other published parameters of the trades. articles.title: Maersk delays Australia and New Zealand no-load policy
articles.summary: Maersk has extended the transition period for its No Shipping Instruction, No Load Policy covering export cargo from Australia and New Zealand. The carrier had planned to begin full enforcement on 30 November 2026, following a soft launch on 2 November. However, the hard-stop date will no longer apply, and Maersk has...
articles.body: Maersk has extended the transition period for its No Shipping Instruction, No Load Policy covering export cargo from Australia and New Zealand. The carrier had planned to begin full enforcement on 30 November 2026, following a soft launch on 2 November. However, the hard-stop date will no longer apply, and Maersk has not yet announced a replacement implementation date. The company said the extension will give customers additional time to establish the required documentation processes and address any outstanding readiness issues with its teams. Under the policy, exporters must submit complete and accurate Shipping Instructions, review the Verify Copy of the bill of lading and complete any necessary amendments before cargo can be confirmed for vessel planning. Maersk had initially required the Shipping Instruction and Verify Copy process to be completed no later than 38 hours before the vessel’s estimated arrival at the applicable load port. The carrier has now placed that 38-hour timeline under review. However, it intends to retain the underlying requirement that Shipping Instructions and verification must be completed before cargo is loaded. During the extended transition period, Maersk will continue working with customers in Australia and New Zealand. The carrier said it will provide advance notice before introducing full enforcement. Once implemented, cargo that has not completed the required documentation process may be excluded from the final load list and rolled to a later vessel. Associated storage, detention, demurrage, handling or rehandling costs may also apply.

articles.title: Russian Military-Linked Cargo Ship Burns After Suspected Drone Strike in Gulf of Finland
articles.summary: A Russian cargo ship linked to Moscow’s military logistics network caught fire after a drone strike in the Gulf of Finland on Saturday, drifting into Finnish territorial waters and triggering...

The vessel later drifted into Finnish territorial waters, prompting a response by Finnish authorities. A Russian cargo ship linked to Moscow’s military logistics network caught fire after a drone strike in the Gulf of Finland on Saturday, drifting into Finnish territorial waters and triggering an emergency maritime rescue operation. The Russian-flagged Sparta II , a sanctioned cargo vessel with a history of transporting military equipment, was struck in international waters west of Gogland Island, known in Finnish as Suursaari, according to Finland’s Ministry of Defence. Finnish military authorities detected the attack at approximately 8:40–8:50 a.m. local time, when the vessel was roughly 50 kilometers west of the island. The damaged ship subsequently lost maneuverability and drifted into Finnish territorial waters, where the Finnish Border Guard assumed responsibility for coordinating rescue operations. The incident took another turn shortly after midday when a Russian helicopter was suspected of entering Finnish airspace near Loviisa, reaching as far as 4.1 kilometers (2.5 miles) into Finnish territory. Finland’s Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen said the suspected airspace violation may have been connected to rescue or surveillance operations involving the damaged cargo ship. “The suspected airspace violation may be related to rescue or monitoring operations concerning the damaged cargo vessel in the Gulf of Finland,” Häkkänen said in a statement translated from Finnish. The Finnish Border Guard is investigating the incident, which occurred at approximately 12:34 p.m. local time. Fire Raises Fears of Explosions and Sinking The Sparta II remained ablaze Saturday afternoon, with Finnish authorities warning that the uncontrolled fire could lead to further explosions or even the loss of the vessel. The Finnish Border Guard said rescue vessels had reached the scene south of Loviisa, where authorities established a restricted area around the damaged ship. An official update issued at 2:58 p.m. local time said the crew had not been forced to abandon the vessel and that no environmental damage had been detected. Finnish authorities were preparing to assist with firefighting, evacuate personnel if necessary, and respond to any marine pollution. In a subsequent briefing reported by Yle, Finnish officials said the ship’s 16 crew members were evacuating into rescue craft. The vessel had anchored at approximately 3:45 p.m., and the anchor was holding. Russian rescue vessels were expected to arrive later Saturday. According to Finnish officials, Russia intended to tow Sparta II back into Russian waters once rescue operations were completed. The Finnish Border Guard emphasized that foreign vessels would require Finnish permission to participate in rescue operations within its area of responsibility. Sanctioned Vessel With Russian Military Connections The roll-on/roll-off Sparta II , IMO 9160994, is associated with Oboronlogistika, a Russian state-linked logistics company that provides maritime transportation services supporting the Russian Ministry of Defence. The vessel has previously been identified as part of Russia’s military logistics network, including operations involving the movement of military equipment between Russian ports and overseas locations. Sparta II was sanctioned by the United States in 2022 over its connections to Oboronlogistika and has been linked to shipments of military equipment from Syria to Russia. The ship has also operated cargo services connecting mainland Russia with its Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad, carrying vehicles, containers and other freight. Despite its military connections, Finnish authorities said they could not confirm whether the vessel was carrying weapons or military equipment when it was attacked. Finland Imposes Air and Maritime Restrictions The drone strike prompted Finland to reintroduce temporary restrictions on aviation and maritime activity in the eastern Gulf of Finland. The Ministry of Defence said the measures were intended to protect civilians and allow authorities to respond to any additional drone threats. Finland also notified its allies of the incident, underscoring the security implications of a military attack taking place near the territorial waters of a NATO member. Finnish authorities said they had received information about Ukrainian drone operations targeting Russia’s Leningrad region earlier Saturday and had taken precautions against drones potentially straying into Finnish territory. Although Finnish officials linked the attack on Sparta II to Ukrainian drones, there was no independently verified confirmation of responsibility from Kyiv in the official statements reviewed. Finland’s Defence Forces said the incident did not represent an immediate military threat to the country and that commercial shipping in the Baltic Sea had not been endangered. War Reaches Another Baltic Shipping Corridor The incident highlights the growing risks to commercial shipping as the war between Russia and Ukraine extends beyond the Black Sea. The Gulf of Finland is one of Russia’s most important maritime corridors, providing access to the Baltic Sea from St. Petersburg and the major oil and cargo terminals at Ust-Luga and Primorsk. It is also a heavily trafficked international shipping route bordered by NATO members Finland and Estonia. Unlike the Black Sea, where merchant vessels have repeatedly been caught up in military operations, the Gulf of Finland has remained a major commercial shipping corridor despite heightened tensions and security concerns since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The attack on Sparta II raises fresh questions about the vulnerability of Russian military-linked shipping in the Baltic and the potential consequences for neighboring countries when damaged vessels drift across maritime boundaries. It also illustrates the challenges facing coastal authorities when a military incident involving a sanctioned foreign vessel develops into a maritime rescue and potential pollution emergency. The Finnish Border Guard said the situation did not pose a danger to other maritime traffic, while rescue and firefighting operations continued in coordination with other authorities. The fate of Sparta II , including whether the damaged ship can be safely towed back to Russian waters, remains uncertain. REUTERS/Caroline Brehman Nov 21 (Reuters) – The Pacific Maritime Association (PMA) employers group at the Los Angeles and Long Beach ports said on Saturday it had reached a tentative agreement with the union for security guards, averting a strike that could have disrupted operations at the two busiest cargo shipping hubs in the US. The International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU) Local 26 represents 250 security officers, or watchmen, who account for a small fraction of the ports’ workforce, but their work is critical because they control access at terminal gates, conduct security patrols and report safety issues. PMA, which represents terminal owners, said the agreement reached on Saturday was subject to ratification by Local 26 members, and the current contract will be extended pending ratification. The union did not immediately respond to a request for comment sent outside regular business hours. The two sides resumed federally mediated negotiations on Friday, two days after the parties broke off talks , with the employers group reporting “little-to-no movement from the union on PMA’s proposals.” The PMA said at the time that its offer included a one-time bonus of $3,200 for each union member and a wage proposal that would raise average annual earnings for full-time watchmen from more than $170,000 to $198,000. The offer also called for maintaining fully employer-paid healthcare for active workers and retirees, valued at more than $62,000 each year, and increased pension benefits up to $93,200 a year for workers with the longest tenure. Talks between the terminal owners and the union have stretched on for more than a year. (Reporting by Akanksha Khushi in Bengaluru, Steve Gorman and Lisa Baertlein in Los Angeles. articles.body: Icelandic shipping and logistics company Eimskip has completed the auction of its new EIM 261130 bond series, accepting bids worth ISK 2.5 billion at a yield of 8.50%. The auction attracted 17 bids with a combined value of ISK 2.7 billion. Submitted yields ranged from 8.20% to 8.75%, while the bonds will be issued at par. The non-indexed bonds have a four-year maturity and will make quarterly interest payments. The first interest payment is scheduled for 26 February 2027, while the principal will be repaid in full when the series matures on 26 November 2030. Each bond has a denomination of ISK 20 million. Payment and settlement are scheduled for 26 November 2026. Eimskip also plans to apply for the admission of the bond series to trading on the Nasdaq Iceland Main Market. Under the terms of the issue, the bonds must be admitted to trading within six months of their issuance and no later than 26 May 2027. Landsbankinn Corporate Finance and Capital Markets managed the auction and will oversee the listing process. articles.body: Fincantieri has signed a contract with Carnival Corporation to build two new dual-fuel cruise ships for Carnival Cruise Line. The vessels will be constructed at the Italian shipbuilder’s Marghera yard, with deliveries scheduled for 2033 and 2035. Each ship will have a gross tonnage of approximately 130,000 GT and around 1,650 guest cabins. The contract is subject to financing and other customary conditions. Fincantieri described its value as significant but did not disclose a financial figure. New vessels to feature LNG propulsion The two cruise ships will feature dual-fuel propulsion systems, with liquefied natural gas (LNG) as their primary fuel. According to Fincantieri, the vessels will combine advanced environmental and digital technologies with an energy-efficient design. The new design has also been developed as a platform that Carnival Corporation could use across several of its cruise brands in the future. The latest order expands a shipbuilding relationship spanning three decades. Fincantieri has delivered 76 vessels to Carnival Corporation’s various cruise brands, including 15 ships for Carnival Cruise Line. “With 12 new ships now on order for delivery through 2039 across Carnival Cruise Line, Princess and AIDA, we have a strong pipeline that supports our measured approach to growth,” said Josh Weinstein, CEO of Carnival Corporation. Weinstein also highlighted the importance of introducing new technologies and improving vessel efficiency as the company expands its fleet. Order adds to Carnival’s existing shipbuilding programme The two new vessels will join Carnival Cruise Line’s existing three-ship Ace-class programme at Fincantieri. Construction of the first Ace-class vessel, Carnival Destiny, began at the shipbuilder’s Monfalcone facility in July 2026. Unlike the newly ordered ships, the Ace-class vessels are being built to a larger design of approximately 230,000 GT. Pierroberto Folgiero, CEO and Managing Director of Fincantieri, said the new contract strengthens the company’s long-term relationship with Carnival Corporation. He also pointed to ongoing investments in shipyard infrastructure, digitalisation, automation and robotics under Fincantieri’s Shipyard of the Future strategy. The latest agreement extends the shipbuilder’s cruise vessel delivery schedule and supports future activity at its Italian facilities.

The warning comes as the Pacific Maritime Association (PMA) and International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU) Local 26 face a critical deadline following more than a year of negotiations over a contract covering approximately 250 port security workers. In a joint statement Friday, the associations called on both sides to remain at the bargaining table, negotiate in good faith and keep cargo moving through the nation’s busiest container port complex. “The Ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach already face congestion from near-record import volumes,” the groups warned, adding that a work stoppage would jeopardize holiday shipments, disrupt manufacturing supply chains and restrict U.S. exports. The statement was backed by major organizations including the National Retail Federation, U.S. Chamber of Commerce, National Association of Manufacturers, American Trucking Associations and more than 100 other groups representing retailers, manufacturers, agricultural producers and logistics providers. The associations warned that a prolonged disruption could quickly spread beyond the waterfront, affecting trucking companies, railroads, warehouses and distribution networks nationwide. Container backlogs could take weeks or months to clear even after operations resume, they said. A Small Union With an Outsized Impact Although Local 26 represents only about 2% of the ILWU workforce at the two ports, its members perform security duties at terminals handling a substantial share of Southern California’s container traffic. According to PMA, the six container terminals covered by the dispute account for approximately 85% of cargo at Long Beach and 33% at Los Angeles. The larger concern is that thousands of longshore workers, marine clerks and foremen covered by separate labor agreements could honor Local 26 picket lines, effectively shutting down cargo operations at affected terminals. PMA warned Wednesday that negotiations held November 17 ended with little progress, while the union had already authorized a strike and indicated it was unwilling to extend the current agreement beyond 12:01 a.m. Pacific time Saturday. The two sides were scheduled to return to the negotiating table Friday in a final effort to avert a work stoppage. articles.body: Vassilis Kikilias at the EPP: “We Cannot Afford to Lose Any More Time – Joint European Action Is Needed on Competitiveness and Shipping” in Hellenic Shipping News 21/11/2026 The need for joint European action to strengthen competitiveness, through the effective implementation of the Draghi Report, was highlighted by Greece’s Minister of Maritime Affairs and Insular Policy, Vassilis Kikilias, in a speech following the conference of the European People’s Party (EPP) Group. The conference was held in Athens at the initiative of Eliza Vozemberg, Chair of the European Parliament’s Committee on Transport and Tourism. The Minister stressed that Europe’s strength lies in its elected representatives, who understand the needs of their respective societies, noting that European institutions and administrative bodies must listen to their positions and proposals and take them seriously. “This is the soul and the heart of European politics. Great European leaders in the past contributed to the creation of our European family and the building of the European idea, recognising that people, societies and states must be at the centre of our policies. And, of course, there must be an institutional and administrative framework that implements the policies of the elected representatives of European countries.” He added: “The Draghi Report, approximately two years ago, marked a turning point in addressing the issues we Europeans had been raising concerning competitiveness, the cost of goods and the prosperity of European families. We must be particularly careful and decisive in implementing policies that serve these objectives.” Referring to the strategic importance of shipping to the global economy, the Minister said: “Greece accounts for 61% of the European fleet and 20% of the global fleet, while 80% of world trade is transported by sea. This is an extremely important fact in understanding what is at stake today in Europe and around the world. “Unfortunately, there is a war at the heart of Europe and another in the Middle East. Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has been disrupted, creating enormous problems for the global economy, as 20% of the world’s oil and 25% of its natural gas pass through it. We are also facing problems with fertiliser supplies. With the war in Ukraine now continuing into its fifth year, we are experiencing even greater difficulties in supply chains, energy and the prices of essential goods. “Therefore, the more we strengthen competitiveness, invest in our ports and shipping, develop our infrastructure and establish an appropriate regulatory framework, the more opportunities we create for growth in our countries, for exporting our products and for prosperity.” As he pointed out, the importance of shipping to national economies and to the everyday lives of European citizens explains Greece’s position on the Net-Zero Framework, both at the IMO and in Europe. “We support the green transition. However, today, liquefied natural gas (LNG) is the transitional fuel, and there is no other available solution, since the quantities of alternative fuels being produced account for just 0.5% of global demand. “We were about to impose an additional financial burden of hundreds of billions of euros on the shipping industry in order to accelerate the green transition using fuels that are not yet available. Had this happened, it would have further fuelled inflation and increased energy and product prices in Europe and across the world. This would have been disastrous for a Europe already under pressure from inflation and facing an energy crisis and a cost-of-living squeeze.” Mr Kikilias went on to discuss the decisive role of ports and their infrastructure in strengthening European competitiveness, stressing: “Our ports are of strategic importance. Why have the United States decided to reinvest in shipyards, shipping, the maritime transportation of energy and ports, and why are China and countries in the East already doing so? Because these sectors will play a decisive role in shaping global power balances and the decisions that will be taken over the next 25 years. “As Europeans, however, we already have this advantage. We have the fleet and we have the ports. This is something we must support. Therefore, when it comes to the Emissions Trading System (ETS), we must take the competitiveness of European ports into account and seek ways to strengthen it, rather than weaken them in comparison with other ports in the Mediterranean or elsewhere in the world.” Concluding his speech, the Minister announced his intention to give shipping a leading role during Greece’s upcoming Presidency of the Council of the European Union, with the participation of representatives of the industry from Greece and across Europe. “As we are due to assume the Presidency of the Council of the European Union in the coming months, I am particularly pleased to announce that we will organise an Informal Meeting of EU Ministers dedicated specifically to shipping. “We will invite the private sector, the President of the Union of Greek Shipowners, Ms Melina Travlou, as well as the leaders of the Greek and European shipping industries, to join you and us – the Members of the European Parliament, members of national parliaments and the Ministry – in meaningful discussions about the future of the sector. “We want to draw on their capabilities so that the many people we represent and support can prosper. This is the way forward, together.” Source: Greek Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Insular Policy 2026-11-21 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: Tanker Market: Arabian Gulf Crude Oil Exports Down 27.6% This Year in Hellenic Shipping News 21/11/2026 T he war in Iran has dealt a significant blow to the Gulf oil export markets, with crude oil loading significantly lower over the 10-month period (Jan.-Oct.). In its latest weekly report, shipbroker Banchero Costa said that “in Jan-Dec 2025, global crude oil loadings went up by +1.8% y-o-y to 2,221.1 mln tonnes, excluding all cabotage trade, according to vessels tracking data from LSEG. This year started well, but the trend reversed from March onwards, and global crude oil loadings in Jan-Oct 2026 were down by -5.8% y-o-y to 1,738.8 mln tonnes. Exports from the Arabian Gulf were down by -27.6% y-o-y to 531.3 mln t in Jan-Oct 2026, accounting for 30.6% of seaborne crude trade, down from 39.8% in the same period of last year. From South America, exports increased by +32.5% y-o-y to 238.8 mln t, with a share of 13.7%. Exports from Russian ports (including oil of Kazakh origin) increased by +6.7% y-o-y in Jan-Oct 2026 to 207.8 mln tonnes, or 12.0% of global trade. From the USA, export volumes increased by +8.5% y-o-y to 166.4 mln t in Jan-Oct 2026, a 9.6% share. From South East Asia exports increased by +2.7% y-o-y to 92.8 mln t in Jan-Oct 2026 (but this inevitably also reflects changes in the re-export of Russian origin volumes)”. According to Banchero Costa, “in terms of demand, the top single country seaborne importer of crude oil in Jan-Oct 2026 was Mainland China, accounting for 18.9% of global trade, although the EU27 as a bloc was a larger buyer. Volumes into China declined by -20.1% y-o-y to 328.4 mln t in Jan-Oct 2026. Imports to the EU27 increased by +0.9% y-o-y to 387.8 mln t, accounting for 22.4% of global trade. To ASEAN, imports declined by -9.2% y-o-y to 219.4 mln t (again this includes Russian volumes later reexported elsewhere in Asia). To India, volumes increased +1.5% y-oy to 200.8 mln t in Jan-Oct 2026”. The shipbroker added that “the Arabian Gulf countries (including Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Iraq and Iran) are the single largest seaborne exporter of crude oil in the world. In 2025 they accounted for 39.8% of global seaborne crude oil exports. In the 12 months of 2025, seaborne crude oil exports from AG countries increased by +1.7% to 883.1 mln tonnes, excluding cabotage, after declining by -0.8% y-o-y in 2024. In Jan-Oct 2026, however, Arabian Gulf crude exports collapsed by -27.6% y-o-y to 531.3 mln tonnes, from 734.1 mln t in the same period of 2025, and their share of global seaborne crude trade fell to 30.6%, from 39.8% a year earlier. About 85.8% of volumes loaded in the AG countries in Jan-Oct 2026 were carried in VLCCs, 11.0% were carried in Suezmaxes, and 3.1% in Aframaxes. These proportions increased in recent years in favour of the largest tankers, as Suezmaxes and Afras were diverted to carry more Russian cargoes”. Meanwhile, “the ranking of export terminals has been transformed by the war in the Gulf, with loadings shifting decisively to terminals that can be reached without transiting the Strait of Hormuz. The main crude oil export terminals in the AG are now: Fujairah (137.8 mln tonnes, or 25.9%, in Jan-Oct 2026), Yanbu (104.0 mln t, or 19.6%), Ras Tanura (59.2 mln t, or 11.1%), Basrah (52.6 mln t, or 9.9%), Sohar (49.8 mln t, or 9.4%), Mina al Fahal (36.7 mln t, or 6.9%), Mina al Ahmadi (14.3 mln t), Zirku Island (11.4 mln t), Das Island (6.1 mln t). Ras Tanura, the largest terminal in the world a year ago, has been overtaken by Fujairah and Yanbu, both of which lie outside the Strait”, Banchero Costa said. “In terms of destinations for crude oil shipments from the AG, the focus in recent years has clearly shifted to Asia. In Jan-Oct 2026, the top destination was South East Asia, accounting for 21.6% of the total AG crude exports, narrowly ahead of Mainland China with 21.5%, followed by India with 14.6%, South Korea with 11.0%, Japan with 7.4%. Direct shipments to the USA now account for just 1.8% of AG exports, and direct shipments to the European Union for just 2.2%. Another 6.1% of AG exports are shipped to the Ain Sukhna Terminal in Egypt to feed the Sumed pipeline, and will eventually mostly end up in Europe. In Jan-Oct 2026, the AG countries shipped 114.4 mln tonnes of crude to Mainland China, which represents a -39.4% y-o-y decline from 188.9 mln tonnesin Jan-Oct 2025. Shipments to South East Asia fell by -27.8% y-o-y to 114.9 mln t, from 159.0 mln t in Jan-Oct 2025. The AG also shipped 77.5 mln t this year to India, which represents a decline of -15.4% y-o-y from 91.6 mln t in the same period last year. Volumes to South Korea declined by -28.4% y-o-y in Jan-Oct 2026 to 58.5 mln t. Shipments from the AG to Japan more than halved, down -52.4% y-o-y in JanOct 2026 to 39.4 mln tonnes”, the shipbroker concluded. articles.title: MEPC 85 to confront net-zero divide
articles.summary: The International Maritime Organization’s Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC 85) will convene in London from Nov 30-Dec 3 against a backdrop of intensifying pressure to deliver a landmark agreement on shipping decarbonisation, with delegates facing what many observers see as a defining moment for the...
articles.body: MEPC 85 to confront net-zero divide in International Shipping News , Shipping: Emission Possible 21/11/2026 T he International Maritime Organization’s Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC 85) will convene in London from Nov 30-Dec 3 against a backdrop of intensifying pressure to deliver a landmark agreement on shipping decarbonisation, with delegates facing what many observers see as a defining moment for the sector’s climate transition. The meeting follows a year of difficult negotiations over the organisation’s proposed mid-term greenhouse gas reduction measures. While the committee’s agenda spans a broad range of environmental issues – including ballast water management, amendments to MARPOL and the NOx Technical Code, marine plastic litter, underwater radiated noise and maritime digitalisation – climate policy is expected to dominate proceedings. Central to those discussions will be efforts to resolve outstanding differences over draft amendments to MARPOL Annex VI and the package of mid-term measures envisioned under the IMO’s 2023 greenhouse gas strategy. According to the IMO, delegates will consider the outcomes of recent intersessional negotiations and seek ways to address “remaining concerns” surrounding the proposed measures, which combine technical and economic elements intended to accelerate emissions reductions from international shipping. The committee is also expected to continue work on the IMO’s Life Cycle GHG Assessment framework. The significance of the discussions has been heightened by the unresolved fate of the IMO’s proposed Net-Zero Framework (NZF), which environmental organisations argue is the industry’s best opportunity to establish a global mechanism for driving down emissions. Adopt ‘as is’ The Clean Shipping Coalition (CSC), representing environmental non-governmental organisations engaged in IMO negotiations, has urged member states to finalise and adopt the framework before the end of the year. “In order to fulfil the goals of the IMO’s GHG Strategy and to protect our global climate, the IMO and all its member states must adopt the Net-Zero Framework ‘as is’, without further diversion,” said Lukas Leppert, president of the Clean Shipping Coalition. “The product of years of negotiations, the Net-Zero Framework reflects findings from the IMO’s Comprehensive Impact Assessment, is a long-negotiated compromise that brings together a multitude of interests and positions, and is supported by a broad majority.” The coalition argues that the framework, originally approved during MEPC 83 in April 2025, already provides a balanced pathway for implementing the IMO’s decarbonisation objectives. The proposed package combines a global fuel standard with an economic mechanism designed to incentivise lower-carbon fuels and technologies. Adoption was delayed after opposition from a group of member states prevented final approval in October 2025. Environmental groups contend that subsequent attempts to replace or significantly revise the framework have failed to attract broad support. “Since October 2025, when IMO member states voted to adjourn the adoption session for one year, various alternative proposals to the NZF were introduced and intensively discussed, but were neither able to demonstrate a comparable reduction in emissions nor gather sufficient support,” Leppert said. “These alternative proposals aimed at supplanting or distracting from the NZF have fallen away, proving the NZF as the best course ahead.” The CSC frames MEPC 85 as a test of the IMO’s ability to convert years of negotiation into binding regulation. “There is no longer time for going in circles; every IMO member state must get behind the Net-Zero Framework and adopt it before the year ends,” Leppert said. EU stance Shipping industry representatives have also taken a view on how member states should proceed. Ahead of the London meetings, Melina Travlos, president of the Union of Greek Shipowners (UGS), warned that political divisions risk undermining efforts to secure a workable global solution. In a statement, she criticised the European Union’s negotiating stance and argued that flexibility remains essential if consensus is to be achieved. “Two months after the inconclusive last round of negotiations at the IMO on reducing greenhouse gas emissions from international shipping, and with the next critical negotiating meetings approaching, there remains no evidence of positive tangible progress,” Travlos said. She argued that recent discussions at European level had demonstrated an unwillingness to compromise, adding that “the EU’s uncompromising position is steering the IMO process to a new dead end, effectively torpedoing the negotiations by depriving them of the flexibility necessary for any chance of success.” The Greek shipowners’ organisation has consistently advocated a global regulatory framework that recognises differing operational realities across shipping segments and trading patterns. Rather than focusing predominantly on alternative fuels, Travlos called for a broader approach incorporating operational and technical efficiency measures. “For a regulation to be effective it must be pragmatic, proportionate and implementable, while reflecting the commercial and operational realities and constraints of the industry,” she said. Travlos further argued that policymakers must align climate ambitions with technological readiness and fuel availability. “This means taking into account the availability, scalability and affordability of alternative fuels, technologies and supporting infrastructure, as well as competing demand from other sectors,” she said. “Such a regulatory framework must also recognise the diversity of solutions available to the shipping industry, rather than focusing exclusively on alternative fuels. It should support all effective pathways to emissions reduction, including technical and operational efficiency measures.” The contrasting positions highlight the challenge awaiting delegates in London. Environmental groups are pressing for rapid adoption of a framework they view as the culmination of years of climate negotiations, while shipowners and several member states are emphasising practicality, flexibility and the risks of imposing measures that outpace technology deployment and fuel availability. After more than a year of delays, MEPC 85 offers member states an opportunity either to bridge their differences and advance a global climate framework or risk prolonging uncertainty over the sector’s pathway to net zero. articles.body: How SAL and DNV are strengthening heavy-lift shipping in International Shipping News 21/11/2026 F rom classification and newbuilding support to operational tools and advisory expertise, SAL and DNV have been collaborating for decades. The partnership supports both the development of SAL’s Orca Class vessels and day-to-day operations, including more efficient cargo planning using DNV’s Route-Specific Cargo Calculator. With a current fleet of 22 DNV-classed heavy-lift vessels, SAL Heavy Lift is a leader in the segment. The Harren Group company’s latest newbuilding programme has set a new benchmark for performance, operational flexibility, and efficiency. Three of a series of five 14,600 dwt Orca Class ships have been delivered so far. SAL is discussing additional newbuilds of the same type with Wuhu Shipyard in China. “Our long-standing collaboration with SAL and Harren Group has covered many different aspects of their fleet,” says Jost Bergmann, Business Director MPV & General Cargo Ships at DNV. Bergmann, who supports SAL’s newbuilding programme for DNV, recently attended the christening of MV Patricia, the third vessel in the series, in Rostock. “The Orca vessels stand out in several respects, both in their design and in how they are intended to support SAL’s operations.” Heavy-lift vessel design built on decades of operational experience The design of SAL’s Orca Class heavy-lift vessels draws on decades of experience in project cargo shipping with a focus on the most demanding cargoes. Developed by SAL’s in-house ship engineering team, the basic design combines the company’s shipbuilding expertise with lessons from operating heavy-lift vessels and transporting complex and oversized cargo. The optimized hull form supports good seakeeping and helps limit acceleration forces acting on the cargo, which can reduce lashing requirements. A forward deck house protects deck cargo from the elements while enabling long cargo, such as wind turbine blades, to extend beyond the stern. Flexible cargo handling for oversized project cargo Cargo flexibility was also a priority. The vessels’ high freeboard helps protect cargo from water, while DNV’s Hatchcoverless class notation allows oversized cargo to be transported in the open hold. A box-shaped single cargo hold and hatch covers designed for loads of up to 10 tonnes per square metre provide additional options for positioning heavy and oversized project cargo. SAL’s requirements for loading flexibility were considered during the design process. DNV’s class-independent Maritime Advisory experts carried out global structural analyses using the vessels’ three-dimensional finite element model to validate these requirements and develop recommendations for optimizing the design. This combination of vessel design and structural analysis supports the operational flexibility required for complex heavy-lift and project cargo. The Orca Class vessels also have a high ice class rating of 1A and Polar Code certification for operations requiring particular care in low ambient temperatures. Electric cranes and flexible propulsion for heavy-lift shipping The vessels combine their cargo capabilities with new crane, energy management, and propulsion technologies. Two fully electric Liebherr Maritime LS 800 E cranes, each with a lifting capacity of 800 tonnes, provide a combined lifting capacity of up to 1,600 tonnes in tandem operation. Using electric rather than hydraulic cranes also eliminates the risk of hydraulic oil escaping from the crane system. A hybrid energy management system combines gensets with lithium-titanium-oxide batteries to optimize energy use. Shore power capability allows the vessels to operate without on-board emissions when suitable infrastructure is available in port. Methanol-ready propulsion for greater fuel flexibility The Orca Class also features a dual-engine concept designed for different operating profiles. One engine supports normal cruising, while the second main engine can provide additional power through the gearbox when required, enabling speeds of up to 18.5 knots for time-critical cargo deliveries. The vessels are designed to be methanol-ready, except for the tanks, allowing conversion for operation with green methanol. Safety and accessibility are also integrated into the design, with stairs providing access to walkways, entrances, accommodation, work areas, and cargo areas. Operational excellence supported by DNV The cooperation between SAL’s parent company Harren Group and DNV extends beyond newbuilding projects. For vessels in operation, Harren Group draws on DNV’s digital class services, software, and class-independent Advisory expertise to support day-to-day fleet management and address technical challenges. My Services on Veracity, for example, gives superintendents and inspectors a central overview of their vessels, helping them monitor the fleet, plan upcoming activities, and arrange surveys easily. Integrated port state control guidance, including relevant checklists and authority focus areas, also helps crews prepare vessels for inspections and smoother port stays. Jan-Hendrik Dammann, Fleet Manager, Harren Shipping Services GmbH & Co. KG, confirms: “DNV’s digital solutions, especially My Services on Veracity, are the benchmark in the market and a real asset in our day-to-day work. For our ships in service, DNV is a partner we can rely on.” The cooperation also gives Harren Group access to DATE (Direct Access to Technical Experts), connecting the company directly with DNV experts when technical questions arise. “We’ve been partners with DNV for a long time, and what we value most is the quality of support and service we receive, online and in person,” highlights Dammann. “We can reach the right experts when needed, and our requests are handled quickly and competently. This close and straightforward cooperation means we usually find joint solutions that are practical and work for both sides.” DNV’s Route-Specific Cargo Calculator delivers solid monetary benefits Carrying extremely heavy or oversized project cargoes comes with stowage restrictions and sea-fastening challenges. Securing breakbulk cargo on board in compliance with the IMO Code of Safe Practice for Cargo Stowage and Securing (CSS Code) requires engineering expertise as well as costly sea-fastening equipment and often comes with considerable efforts for deck reinforcements. Intended to predict the acceleration forces acting on the cargo during transit, the CSS Code assumes the harsh conditions in the North Atlantic, and uses standardized ship contours. But for trips in much more benign sea areas, these rules are overly conservative. While calculating the more realistic accelerations along a given route takes expert knowledge, DNV’s Route-Specific Cargo Calculator tool on Veracity provides a convenient, user-friendly way for cargo planners to predict the acceleration forces during the relevant season without requiring engineering skills. Increased stowage flexibility and capacity utilization SAL is using the tool more and more, says Karsten Behrens, Managing Director at SAL Engineering. “It gives us greater stowage flexibility compared to the CSS Code, for example in matching the vessel with the cargo or placing cargo on the weather deck. It also reduces the lashing effort and expense. These effects can multiply when identical cargo is transported along the same route repeatedly.” In one case, the tool helped SAL make better use of the available space on board by calculating a reduced route- and season-specific maximum transverse acceleration of 3.95 m/s2, which is roughly 75 per cent of the assumed value according to the CSS Code of 5.23 m/s2. The resulting reduction of deck loads allowed 15 to 20 per cent more cargo to be transported on that voyage. “In some cases the DNV tool allows us to accept a particular shipping order; in other cases, it reduces the number of trips we must take,” says Behrens. “This is in the best interests of both the cargo owner and the ship operator.” Stored digital ship model reduces lashing time and effort The Route-Specific Cargo Calculator uses a digital model of the ship that has to be entered into DNV’s Veracity system only once. All the user has to enter for a specific trip are some loading condition parameters like draft, trim, and metacentric height (GM), the stowage positions of cargo items, plus the route and, optionally, the season. The tool uses its database of route-specific sea states to return realistic acceleration values. “While we could calculate these values ourselves at SAL Engineering,” remarks Behrens, “the DNV tool reduces the effort and speeds up the process, freeing up our resources for other purposes.” Another typical use case is transporting wind turbine components from the U.S. East Coast to Mexico. The CSS Code would require extensive lashing, but sailing this route during the summer season reduces the lashing requirement by about 50 per cent. RSCC unlocks operational potential and strengthens risk management “The DNV tool helps open up untapped potential,” explains Behrens. “What is more, even in the North Atlantic in winter, when we operate under the most severe conditions, the tool gives us reassurance that the sea-fastening and loading measures we take are on the safe side. For shipments with our newbuild MV Elise, we not only knew that we were on the safe side, but the tool even told us how far.” Source: DNV, https://www.dnv.com/expert-story/maritime-impact/how-sal-and-dnv-are-strengthening-heavy-lift-shipping/ Tops 2026-11-21 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share
takeaways: The partnership supports both the development of SAL’s Orca Class vessels and day-to-day operations, including more efficient cargo planning using DNV’s Route-Specific Cargo Calculator.
With a current fleet of 22 DNV-classed heavy-lift vessels, SAL Heavy Lift is a leader in the segment.

Peter Sand, Xeneta Chief Analyst: “Offered capacity is increasing on all fronthauls out of the Far East to Europe and the US, with average spot rates unsurprisingly continuing to soften – with one exception. The trade from the Far East to the Mediterranean is moving in mysterious ways, with spot rates increasing 6.8% in the past week. “Average spot rates into the Mediterranean are now USD 1,551 per FEU higher than into North Europe. That trend has now turned, with the seven-day average falling 28% from a peak of 16.6 transits per day on 25 October to 11.9 on 19 November. “Something has happened to cool the return of container shipping services to the Red Sea in November. Whatever the reason, disruption in the Red Sea is felt more acutely on trades between the Far East and the Mediterranean because they are the most operationally exposed to the region. “This is a timely reminder to shippers that the path to forecasted falling freight rates in 2027 will not be plain sailing. articles.summary: After several weeks of improving confidence, recycling buyers are beginning to have second thoughts about how aggressively to pursue fresh tonnage. Bangladesh’s recent optimism has been tempered by weaker steel, political unrest and sluggish domestic demand, prompting some buyers to reconsider their purchasing ideas...
articles.body: GMS Week 47 – The Tide Of Second Thoughts in Weekly Demolition Reports 21/11/2026 After several weeks of improving confidence, recycling buyers are beginning to have second thoughts about how aggressively to pursue fresh tonnage. Bangladesh’s recent optimism has been tempered by weaker steel, political unrest and sluggish domestic demand, prompting some buyers to reconsider their purchasing ideas or delay commitments. Elsewhere, sentiment remains selective rather than distressed. Recycling indications are unchanged across all four destinations, although the shortage of available candidates continues to restrict fresh business. Dry freight surrendered part of last week’s gains, with the Baltic Dry Index easing from 3,020 on November 12 to 2,901 on Thursday, November 19. Capesizes declined to 4,514 and Supramaxes slipped to 1,814, while Panamaxes edged higher to 2,132. Despite the correction, employment opportunities remain sufficiently attractive for many ageing vessels, limiting the incentive for owners to consider recycling. Crude oil continued its downward trajectory, with Brent trading around USD 90 per barrel on Friday and WTI near USD 82. Recovering Middle Eastern exports and expectations of greater supply have outweighed continuing regional security concerns. Lower energy costs may provide some relief to recyclers and steel producers, although uncertain Gulf trading conditions continue to influence vessel employment and disposal decisions. Regional steel markets offered mixed signals. Bangladesh plate retreated from last week’s improvement, while Indian steel recovered towards Friday and Pakistani prices strengthened marginally. Chinese quotations weakened further. These movements have provided little justification for stronger recycling bids, particularly where domestic finished-steel consumption remains disappointing. Bangladesh faces the week’s most challenging domestic developments, with political unrest, disruptions in the garment sector and weak local demand prompting greater buyer caution. India continues to pursue specialist opportunities and has sought Italian support for European approval of selected recycling facilities. Pakistan remains measured, while Turkey faces subdued steel demand and continuing production disruption at a major mill. Waterfront activity nevertheless continued. Alang and Chattogram recorded further arrivals and deliveries, while Gadani received another bulker. These movements primarily reflect previously secured tonnage rather than fresh transactions. No new recycling sales were reported during the week. The market therefore enters the final weeks of November with buyers reassessing their positions rather than abandoning them. Bangladesh’s earlier enthusiasm has given way to greater caution, while India, Pakistan and Turkey remain selective. Owners, meanwhile, still have sufficient trading alternatives to resist recycling. The price board has not moved, but the conviction behind it is being tested. For now, the market is not changing its prices. It is having second thoughts about paying them. articles.body: Drewry: World Container Index Down 3% Last Week in International Shipping News 21/11/2026 For many years, World Container Index (WCI) has been the go-to, independent, global reference for index-linked contracts. If your organisation requires regional visibility/coverage beyond the eight trade lanes provided below, contact the team. Our detailed assessment for Thursday, 19 Nov 2026 • The Drewry World Container Index (WCI), the benchmark widely referenced by procurement teams, decreased 3% to $4,176 per 40ft container this week due to declining rates on the Transpacific trade route. Despite the decline, the WCI remains 126% higher YoY. • On the Transpacific trade route, rates continued their downwards trend for the seventh consecutive week. Rates from Shanghai to New York decreased 9% to $8,194 per 40ft container, the lowest in 15 weeks, and those from Shanghai to Los Angeles fell 5% to $7,026 per 40ft container, the lowest in 12 weeks. In response to the weak demand, carriers are reducing capacity through blank sailings. According to Drewry’s Container Capacity Insight, ten blank sailings have been announced for next week, compared with four this week. Despite these capacity reductions, Drewry expects freight rates to decrease further next week. • On the Asia-Europe/Med trade route, rates from Shanghai to Genoa increased 6% to $4,436 per 40ft container after remaining stable for three consecutive weeks, while Shanghai to Rotterdam rates remained unchanged at $3,496 per 40ft container. Carriers are managing capacity through blank sailings, and according to Drewry’s Container Capacity Insight, four blank sailings are announced for next week, lower than five this week. As demand is expected to strengthen in December ahead of the new contract season, many carriers have announced PSS, ranging from $1,000-1,600 per 40ft container on Asia-Europe/Med effective December. Hence, Drewry expects rates to increase in the coming weeks. • The East-West container shipping market remains under pressure, with different trends on Transpacific and Asia-Europe/Med trade routes. Asia–Europe demand is expected to strengthen in December ahead of the new contract season and Chinese New Year, prompting carriers to push rate increases through surcharges, whereas easing Transpacific demand is likely to drive rates lower. Meanwhile, worsening North Europe port congestion is delaying empty-container returns to Asia, raising concerns over future equipment shortages. Suez Canal transits improved to 57 vessels last week, while only four vessels crossed the Strait of Hormuz. With geopolitical uncertainty and potential labour disruptions at Los Angeles and Long Beach remain key risks, shippers should expect continued rate volatility. articles.title: Iran War Oil Premium Evaporates as Global Crude Supplies Surge
articles.summary: The price of US sour oil has plunged, as a surge in crude supply from Venezuela, Canada and the Middle East gives refiners ample barrels to choose from.
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network Photo: Shutterstock/Sven Hansche By Nathan Risser and Yongchang Chin (Bloomberg) –The price of US sour oil has plunged, as a surge in crude supply from Venezuela, Canada and the Middle East gives refiners ample barrels to choose from. US medium sour export grade Mars traded at a record premium to benchmark West Texas Intermediate futures in the early days of the Iran war. Buyers turned to the Gulf of Mexico variety, which is similar in quality to Middle Eastern crude, as the closure of the Strait of Hormuz disrupted supplies. Now, as oil markets begin to settle after a volatile year, Mars has fallen to a deep discount, making it cheaper for US refiners built to process heavier crude. Mars has dropped from a $10 premium to a $4 discount to WTI futures in less than a month. That’s the steepest discount since late September. Mars rallied to record premium of $17.50 at the peak of supply disruptions in March and April. At the start of the year, before the US and Israel launched their war in Iran in late February, the grade largely traded at a discount. Rising production of heavy-sour crude in Venezuela and Canada has pushed global prices lower in recent weeks. US refiners, major buyers of heavier oil along the Gulf Coast and in the Midwest, have benefited from increased supplies from Canada and Latin America. At the same time, higher shipping costs are weighing on prices at the barrel’s origin by making overseas sales more expensive. Flows from the Persian Gulf have also increased. Higher Middle Eastern flows, however, have reduced the incentive for Asian refiners to take advantage of falling Mars prices, with the US grade still uneconomical to import, according to traders familiar with the matter, who asked not to be named because they aren’t authorized to speak to the media. On a delivered basis to Northeast Asia, Mars for February was priced at a premium of about $12 to $13 a barrel to the Dubai benchmark — around $10 more expensive than similar quality oil from Saudi Arabia, they said. At least one other seller of Middle Eastern crude has also slashed offer prices, they added. “Incremental supply looks to be dominated by heavier and more sour barrels, especially out of Canada, Venezuela, and the Middle East,” Valero’s head of crude supply Randy Hawkins said in an October earnings call. It’s a “race to the bottom” Phillips 66’s executive vice president of marketing and commercial Brian Mandell said on a call with analysts the same month. In Canada, the pipeline that takes oil sands crude from inland fields to export markets on the West Coast is operating at a record 960,000 barrels a day this month, 8% above its stated capacity. Oil will also be shipped on 34 vessels out of the Westridge terminal near Vancouver in November, up from 31 in October. While cheaper heavy crude is a boon to refiners who are already making record profits from the Iran war’s disruptions to global fuel markets, it is coming at a cost to heavy oil producers. “We’re basically going to have to be a price taker,” oil driller Sable Offshore Corp. chief executive office Jim Flores said earlier this month. Sable pumps heavy oil off the coast of California. For now, US crude exports of both heavy and light grades continue at historically elevated levels. US crude exports averaged 4 million barrels a day over the past four weeks, below the weekly record of more than 6 million set in April but well above the 3 million average since the US lifted its crude-export ban in 2015. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. articles.body: Oil Prices Drop for Third Week Straight Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 20, 2026 © Adobe Stock/Zulfugar Karimov Oil prices fell on Friday and were set for a weekly decline on strong exports from the Middle East despite Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia's capital Riyadh and reports of tanker disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz. Brent crude futures were down 67 cents, or 0.7%, at $91.31 a barrel at 1414 GMT. US West Texas Intermediate futures for December were down 36 cents, or 0.4%, at $82.85 a barrel, while the more active January contract was down 19 cents, or 0.2%, at $82.85. Brent is on track for a near 5% decline for the week and the December WTI contract for a 6.5% weekly drop as expectations of a supply surplus grew because crude shipments through the Strait of Hormuz have returned to roughly pre-war levels. This would be the benchmarks' third straight week of decline. "This week we keep having relatively strong export flows out of the Middle East. There is also a narrative ongoing that as long as people are talking, maybe there's a deal in the making," said Aldo Spanjer, commodity strategist at BNP Paribas. "The prices are correct if you believe that this geopolitical risk doesn't come back. I'm not in that camp who thinks this is done ... I probably see a rebound," he said. On Friday, the Iran-aligned Houthi movement warned workers and people near Saudi Arabia's Red Sea ports to evacuate immediately and urged shipping companies to remove vessels, saying they would target Saudi ports in Jeddah and the Red Sea if a Saudi-led coalition strikes Yemen's Hodeidah port. The Houthis fired missiles at Riyadh on Thursday. Two oil tankers also hit naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz and "are burning," Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy said in a statement carried by state media on Thursday. Iran's intensifying attacks on tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz, "running at roughly one incident per day in November," still add a meaningful geopolitical risk premium to the market, according to UOB Group analysts in a client note. OPEC+ ministers will hold a series of meetings on November 29 to decide their 2027 output policy. The group comprises the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and allies such as Russia. The Middle East conflict has caused the biggest disruption ever to global oil and gas trade and could cut world oil demand by more than 4% by 2035 if governments accelerate electrification, efficiency and fuel-switching measures in response, the International Energy Agency said on Thursday. However, some analysts expect softness in the broader equities markets to weigh on oil prices, as Asian shares fell on Friday — heading for their worst week since 2020. "Supply disruptions remain a risk, but near-term demand concerns tied to the AI trade unwind and broader risk-off sentiment are weighing on prices," said Saxo analysts in a note. In Russia, crude oil output could fall again as Ukrainian attacks on refineries and export infrastructure intensify, analysts and traders say. Ukrainian drone a ttacks have cut Russian oil refineries' combined crude processing volumes by 45% since late October, Reuters reported on Wednesday. (Reuters)

articles.summary: US Treasury Department officials met with government authorities in Singapore and Malaysia this week, including regulators and national security bodies, to warn of potential risks they could face if they do not comply with US sanctions on Iran.Washington is urging the countries…
articles.body: US Treasury Urges Singapore, Malaysia of Compliance With Iran Sanctions Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 20, 2026 © Adobe Stock/christianthiel.net US Treasury Department officials met with government authorities in Singapore and Malaysia this week, including regulators and national security bodies, to warn of potential risks they could face if they do not comply with US sanctions on Iran. Washington is urging the countries, as well as law firms and banks operating there, to stay alert for Iranian front companies, as it steps up efforts to enforce sanctions in Asia and bring about a speedy end to the conflict in the Middle East. The US is urging additional scrutiny on "high-risk" sectors such as maritime transport, aviation services and procurement networks, "to make sure they're not fronting for Iran," said a Treasury Department official. "We want it to be understood too, that we're going to target these lifelines, and it's not going to be a negotiation when we find a lifeline that needs to be targeted," the official said. Since the US and Israel commenced strikes on Iran in February, the US has intensified actions to throttle Tehran's business interests overseas. In August, President Donald Trump's administration launched Operation Economic Outcast, resulting in a barrage of sanctions against targets spanning Canadian digital currency platforms to a major Russian banking group. OIL ON WATER For years, tankers have regularly made stops in the waters around Malaysia, Singapore and Indonesia to make ship-to-ship transfers of Iranian oil that help obscure its origin. REUTERS/Stringer Another tanker was struck by a projectile and caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz on Friday, extending a wave of attacks on commercial shipping that has pushed maritime security incidents to their highest weekly level since mid-October. The tanker was transiting outbound through the strategic waterway when an unknown projectile struck its port bow, sparking a fire onboard. The vessel’s company security officer reported no casualties or environmental impact. Authorities are investigating. The attack comes amid a sharp escalation in threats to merchant shipping across the Middle East and Black Sea. According to maritime security analyst Martin Kelly of Orbital Risk Intelligence, shipping experienced 15 attacks and piracy-related incidents over the past seven days, a 50% increase from the previous week and the highest weekly total since mid-October. In the Persian Gulf, Strait of Hormuz and Gulf of Oman, Kelly recorded seven strikes involving six vessels. Four tankers were hit within 13 nautical miles of Khasab over three days, including the LPG tanker TARA GAS , which was attacked twice. The violence has left two seafarers missing and 13 injured, according to Kelly’s assessment. Among the most serious incidents was the November 17 attack on the tanker NAVIG8 MESSI , which suffered a fire after being struck 13 nautical miles north of Khasab. ADNOC confirmed that one crew member was missing and 11 others were injured. The remaining crew were evacuated and the vessel was reported under tow. The TARA GAS , meanwhile, was disabled by a projectile strike on November 16 before being hit again the following day, resulting in another fire and the vessel being abandoned. The deteriorating security situation is taking a continued toll on commercial traffic. Combined traffic remains approximately 65% below pre-conflict levels. UKMTO recorded six verified attacks across the Strait of Hormuz and Persian Gulf during its latest reporting period, which covered incidents through November 18. Four occurred in the Strait itself and two in the wider Persian Gulf. Two vessels required assistance, while the outcomes of four others remained unknown. Since the U.S.-Iran ceasefire agreement expired on August 17, UKMTO has recorded six total vessel losses, while 22 vessels required assistance and 31 were confirmed to have continued their voyages. The Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) continues to assess the threat to commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz as SEVERE , warning that further deliberate attacks are highly likely. The surge in maritime violence extends well beyond the Middle East. Piracy-related activity has also increased in the Gulf of Aden and western Indian Ocean. In another incident off Al Mukalla, armed guards aboard a cargo vessel fired a warning shot to repel an attempted boarding. The ship’s security team returned warning shots, forcing the attackers to retreat. No injuries or damage were reported. The incidents underscore the growing range of threats facing merchant vessels, from projectile and drone attacks in active conflict zones to renewed piracy activity along established trading routes. With attacks concentrated around the Strait of Hormuz and the western Black Sea, maritime security analysts warn that the coming week could bring further strikes against commercial vessels. Join the leading maritime news network Illustration: Shutterstock South Korean shipbuilder Samsung Heavy Industries and U.S. nuclear technology company Tesser Atomics have signed an exclusive agreement to develop a nuclear-powered LNG carrier intended for commercial service between the United States and Europe. The memorandum of understanding, signed November 19, establishes Samsung Heavy Industries as the exclusive shipbuilding partner and Tesser Atomics as the exclusive reactor technology partner for the demonstration project, which aims to develop the world’s first nuclear-powered LNG carrier. The collaboration brings together Samsung’s ship design and construction capabilities with Tesser’s advanced reactor technology as the companies work toward demonstrating nuclear propulsion on an established commercial trade route. At the center of the project is Tesser’s Triton reactor, a compact fluoride-salt-cooled high-temperature reactor designed specifically for marine applications. The system uses TRISO nuclear fuel and low-pressure molten salt coolant, with a design that allows refueling while the reactor remains in operation. The companies say the technology could provide the power needed to propel large oceangoing vessels without relying on conventional marine fuels. “Demonstrating nuclear propulsion on an LNG carrier crossing the Atlantic would open new horizons for decarbonizing the shipping industry,” said Kyunghee Kim, Executive Vice President and Head of the Future Business Division at Samsung Heavy Industries. The project builds on Norway’s NuProShip research program, which evaluated advanced reactor technologies for merchant vessels, and is being advanced through SFI SAINT, a research consortium led by the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU) and supported by the Research Council of Norway. The Norwegian initiative is targeting several nuclear-powered vessel demonstrations in the early 2030s, including an LNG carrier project backed by shipowner Knutsen OAS. Samsung Heavy Industries is no stranger to nuclear-powered LNG carrier development. In September 2025, the shipbuilder and the Korea Atomic Energy Research Institute secured Approval in Principle from ABS and the Liberian flag state for a separate LNG carrier concept powered by a 100-megawatt-thermal molten salt reactor. The latest agreement represents another step toward moving nuclear propulsion beyond conceptual designs and into commercial demonstration. However, significant hurdles remain. Nuclear-powered merchant ships face complex requirements involving reactor licensing, maritime safety, port access, crew training, insurance and liability. The International Maritime Organization is currently working to modernize its regulatory framework for nuclear-powered ships, with adoption of a revised Nuclear Code and amendments to SOLAS Chapter VIII targeted for 2030. The economics also remain uncertain. An ABS-supported study published in October found that a nuclear-powered LNG carrier could cost roughly 2.5 times as much to build as a conventional vessel, although lower fuel costs could improve its long-term economics. For now, the Samsung-Tesser agreement remains a development partnership rather than a firm shipbuilding order. The companies have not disclosed a construction schedule, vessel specifications, project cost or financing arrangements. Still, the project adds to growing efforts by shipbuilders, reactor developers and maritime regulators to determine whether nuclear propulsion can become a commercially viable alternative for deep-sea shipping. The agreement, valued at more than €2 billion ($2.2 billion), calls for construction of two dual-fuel cruise ships at Fincantieri’s Marghera shipyard in Italy, with deliveries scheduled for 2033 and 2035. Each vessel will measure approximately 130,000 gross tons and feature around 1,650 passenger cabins. The ships will primarily operate on liquefied natural gas (LNG) and incorporate advanced environmental and digital technologies. Carnival Cruise Line President Christine Duffy said the new ships will complement the company’s existing fleet of 29 vessels. “With a 29-ship fleet, we know our guests appreciate choices,” Duffy said. “They love the incredible experiences and amenities on our Excel Class ships, the largest in our fleet, but they also love the intimacy our smaller ships offer.” Fincantieri said the design has also been developed as a multi-brand platform, potentially allowing Carnival Corporation to adopt the same basic vessel design across several of its cruise lines in the future. November 20, 2026 © Dongara Marine The Cook Labor Government is investing $13.4 million in two new vessels to strengthen fisheries compliance and protect the Kimberley's valuable marine resources. A new nine-meter amphibious vessel is now operating out of Broome, undertaking patrols across the Buccaneer Archipelago Marine Park. The vessel was built by global business Sealegs who specialize in manufacturing the versatile craft. The vessel's ability to travel on both land and water will allow Fisheries and Marine Officers to access remote locations where extreme tidal conditions and limited boat ramp infrastructure can make launching traditional vessels difficult. The vessel will support joint patrols with local Aboriginal ranger groups, strengthening partnerships and supporting the shared management of the culturally significant region. The larger 22-meter patrol vessel will also be based in Broome, supporting commercial and recreational fisheries compliance and marine park management across northern waters. Expected to be delivered in October 2028, the new vessel will be built by Dongara Marine, providing another boost to Western Australia's marine manufacturing industry. November 20, 2026 © Hatenboer-Water Hatenboer-Water has started building a new headquarters in Schiedam, driving the first foundation pile on Thursday after early demolition work. Due to finish in the third quarter of 2027, the new building project adds manufacturing space and twice the company's current testing capacity as orders grow across shipping and offshore energy. Hatenboer-Water's existing premises in Schiedam have reached their limit. Rebuilding on site upgrades its engineering workshops and manufacturing facilities and keeps the business inside the Port of Rotterdam maritime cluster. Schiedam's focus on maritime manufacturing puts the company close to European shipbuilders, engineering firms and offshore service providers. The site also serves as the main hub for regional offices in Aberdeen, Dubai, Houston, Singapore and Hamburg. Doubling production and testing capacity means Hatenboer-Water can build more systems and run several demanding tests simultaneously, cutting waiting times and speeding up delivery. Inside, the building includes new production equipment, a better layout for moving materials, shared meeting spaces for visiting clients, and upgraded IT infrastructure and access controls. Separate, fully secured office zones with restricted access will let teams work on confidential projects. Designed as an all-electric, fully insulated building, it will also operate without natural gas. Daily operations will not stop during construction. Using a phased 'chessboard' plan, the existing building will stay in use while the first new sections are built. Staff and equipment will move across step by step as each part finishes, keeping production and support running as normal through 2027.

articles.body: Vice Adm. Burdian appointed as DHS Joint Task Force-Maritime Director Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 20, 2026 Vice Adm. Jo‑Ann Burdian. Image courtesy USCG Vice Adm. Jo‑Ann Burdian was presidentially appointed as the director, Department of Homeland Security Joint Task Force–Maritime (JTF-M), effective Nov. 10, 2026. DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin nominated Burdian as director of JTF-M, in accordance with 6 U.S.C. § 348(b)(3)(A), to ensure the critical, continued role of JTF-M in synchronizing multi-agency maritime operations and securing the nation’s maritime borders. “Vice Admiral Burdian’s appointment as the JTF-M director marks a pivotal moment for our collective maritime defense," said Mullin. "Her unmatched operational expertise is critical as JTF-M continues to dismantle illicit networks, prevent hostile exploitation of our maritime borders, and leverage the MOC-P construct to achieve departmental unity of effort and drive nationwide success." JTF-M synchronizes DHS component operations, intelligence, and investigations across the maritime domain to secure U.S. borders, prevent and respond to homeland security crises and facilitate regionally based joint operations. As the DHS Maritime Operations Coordination Plan (MOC-P) program office, JTF-M enhances coordination among DHS components, eliminating redundancy and increasing effectiveness through 35 Regional Coordinating Mechanisms (ReCoMs). These ReCoMs execute DHS missions at every major U.S. port, along all U.S. coastlines and approaches to maritime borders of the U.S. and its territories. The ReCoMs help prevent terrorist, criminal, and hostile activities and dismantle illicit networks attempting to exploit the maritime domain and reduce vulnerabilities while safeguarding legal trade and travel. "I am honored to lead the dedicated staff of Joint Task Force-Maritime as we strengthen our borders and streamline interagency response," said Burdian. "Through our 35 ReCoMs and strong partnerships with the Department of War, we will continue to safeguard legal trade and travel while remaining an impenetrable barrier against cross-border smuggling, illegal immigration and illicit trafficking." Burdian also serves as commander, Coast Guard Atlantic Area and commander, Coast Guard Defense Force East, providing Coast Guard forces and operations across all mission areas from the Arctic Ocean to the Arabian Gulf in support of the DoW and combatant commanders for national defense missions.
